meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'It matters not how strait the gate, how charged with punishments the scroll'?
meta.ogDescription: A rare case where the famous name is right: this is Henley's own line from the final stanza of "Invictus" (published 1888).

answer.label: Written by
answer.sourceLine: This is a genuine Henley line — the opening couplet of the fourth and final stanza of his poem later titled “Invictus.” He wrote it in 1875 while hospitalised in Edinburgh, and it first appeared in print in his A Book of Verses (1888). The wording — “It matters not how strait the gate, / How charged with punishments the scroll” — is exact.

source.heading: The source

docMeta.dd: A Book of Verses, in the sequence “Life and Death (Echoes)”

source.excerpt:
Out of the night that covers me,
Black as the Pit from pole to pole,
I thank whatever gods may be
For my unconquerable soul.

…

It matters not how strait the gate,
How charged with punishments the scroll,
I am the master of my fate:
I am the captain of my soul.
trail: The line is the last stanza of “Invictus” — see the full text at the Academy of American Poets.
Henley wrote it in 1875 and first published it, untitled, in A Book of Verses (1888); the title “Invictus” was added later by editor Arthur Quiller-Couch, per Wikipedia.
The exact wording — “how strait the gate, / How charged with punishments the scroll” — matches the standard published text at the Poetry Foundation.
source.excerptNote: The quoted line opens the poem’s famous closing quatrain; “strait” (narrow) echoes the “strait gate” of Matthew 7:14.

source.rightsNote: “Invictus” was first published in 1888 in Henley’s A Book of Verses, and Henley died in 1903. As a work published well before 1931 it is in the public domain in the United States.

author.name: William Ernest Henley
author.heading: About the author
author.bio: William Ernest Henley was an English poet, editor and critic who lost a leg to tuberculosis of the bone as a young man and spent years in hospital fighting to keep the other. He wrote “Invictus” from that sickbed in 1875. As an editor he championed writers including Kipling, Yeats and H. G. Wells, and his robust personality partly inspired his friend Robert Louis Stevenson’s Long John Silver.

misattribution.heading: So is it really his?
misattribution.intro: Unusually for a much-shared line, this one is authentic: it really is Henley’s own writing. The confusions that surround it are about the poem’s title and its later famous admirers, not its authorship.

items.why: Henley published the poem untitled in 1888. The now-inseparable Latin title “Invictus” (“unconquered”) was supplied by editor Arthur Quiller-Couch when he included it in the Oxford Book of English Verse (1900), per Wikipedia.
Mandela famously drew strength from “Invictus” on Robben Island and popularised it anew, which leads some to credit him with the words. He recited and loved the poem — he did not write it.

misattribution.truthLine: The words are genuinely William Ernest Henley’s, from the closing stanza of the poem we now call “Invictus” — read the full text.

context.heading: Why it endures
lead: “Invictus” is one of the most quoted Victorian poems in English, and this couplet is its emotional hinge: whatever narrow gate or ledger of punishments awaits, the speaker claims mastery over fate and soul. Henley wrote it not as abstract bravado but from a hospital bed, having already lost one leg and fighting to save the other.

The poem has since been invoked in wildly different contexts — by Nelson Mandela in prison, in political speeches, in the 2009 film named for it — a reach that keeps its final lines in constant circulation.
